en: The Questions of King Milinda,
Chapter on Time, Section 6:
The Question on the Unity and Diversity of Name-and-Form (Nāmarūpa)
The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, who is it that undergoes rebirth?
The Elder replied:
“Name-and-form, Great King, is what undergoes rebirth-linking.
“But is it this very same name-and-form that undergoes rebirth-linking?

“It is not this very same name-and-form, Great King, that undergoes rebirth-linking. Rather, Great King, by means of this name-and-form one performs karma—whether beautiful or evil—and by that karma another name-and-form undergoes rebirth-linking.”
“Venerable sir, if it is not this very name-and-form that undergoes rebirth-linking, will he not indeed be freed from evil kamma?
The Elder said:
“If it were not to undergo rebirth-linking, he would be freed from evil kamma.”
"But because, Great King, one undergoes rebirth, therefore one is not released from evil deeds.
"Give me an illustration," [the king said].
"Suppose, Great King, some man were to steal another man's mango; then that man..."
Taking both mangoes, he would show them to the king, saying: “Sire, this man has carried off my mangoes.

He would then say: “Sire, I did not carry off this man’s mangoes; those mangoes which were planted by him are one thing, and those mangoes which were carried off by me are another. I have not incurred punishment.”
“Would that man, Great King, deserve punishment?
“Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.
“For what reason?”
“Even though he might say that, Bhante, by not relinquishing the former mango, that man would still be liable to punishment for the later mango.

“In the same way, Great King, one performs action—whether beautiful or evil—with this present name-and-form; by means of that action, another name-and-form is reborn. Therefore, one is not released from evil deeds.
“Give me a further simile.”
“Just as, great king, some man might steal another man’s rice...
[or] steal his sugarcane...
just as, great king, some man, having lit a fire in the winter season to warm himself, might depart without extinguishing it;”
Then that fire might burn the field of a certain man; the owner of the field would seize him and present him to the king, saying, "Sire, this man has burned my field.
He would say, "Sire, I did not set this man's field on fire. That fire which was ignited by me is one thing, and that fire by which his field was burned is another. I am not subject to punishment."
“Would that man, Great King, deserve punishment?
“Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.
“For what reason?”
“Even though he might speak thus, venerable sir, that man would still be liable to punishment for not having renounced the former fire when he used the latter fire.

“In the same way, great king, one performs action—whether beautiful or evil—with this name-and-form; by means of that action, another name-and-form is reborn. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.
“Give me a further simile.”
“Suppose, great king, a certain man were to take a lamp, ascend a palace, and eat.
While the lamp burns, it might set fire to some grass; the burning grass might set fire to the house; the burning house might set fire to the village.
Then the people of the village, having seized that man, might say: ‘Why, good man, did you [set fire to] the village?’”
‘I have burnt down the village,’ he might say, ‘Sir, I did not burn down the village;
that was the lamp-fire by whose light I ate, and that is a different fire by which the village was burnt.
If they were to come into your presence disputing thus, O Great King, whose case would you uphold?”
“Of the village folk, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Even though he might say that, nevertheless, it was from that very source that the fire arose.”

“In the same way, Great King, although the name-and-form at the end of life is one thing and the name-and-form at rebirth-linking is another, nevertheless, that [rebirth] is produced from that very [previous state]; therefore, one is not freed from evil kamma.
“Give me a further simile,” he said.
“Suppose, Great King, some man were to take a young girl as a wife, pay the bride-price, and then depart.”

At a later time, she would have grown up and reached maturity; then another man, having paid the bride-price, would take her in marriage. The other [first] man, arriving, might say: "Why, good man, have you taken my wife?
He would reply: "I am not taking your wife. That girl was young and tender whom you chose and for whom you paid the bride-price;
this is another girl who has grown up and reached maturity, whom I have chosen and for whom I have paid the bride-price."
"And suppose," he said, "those disputing were to come into your presence.
Whose case, Great King, would you uphold?
"The former one, Bhante."
“For what reason?
[The King asked. “Even though he might say that, nevertheless, it was produced from that very source.

“In the same way, O Great King, although the name-and-form at the time of death is one thing and the name-and-form at rebirth-linking is another, nevertheless, it was produced from that very source; therefore, one is not released from evil kamma.”
“Give me another simile.

“Suppose, great king, a certain man were to buy a jar of milk from a cowherd’s hand, leave it in that very person’s hand, and depart, thinking, ‘I will come back tomorrow and take it. On the following day, it would have turned into curds.
Having returned, he would say, ‘Give me my jar of milk.’”
He would show him the curd.
The other might say, "I am not buying curd from your hand; give me a jar of milk.
He might reply, "Since you did not know it, the milk has turned into curd. If they were to come before you, Your Majesty, disputing in this way, whose case would you uphold?"
“Because of Gopālaka, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Even though he might say that, nevertheless, it was produced from that very source.”

“In the same way, great king, although the name-and-form at the end of life is one thing and the name-and-form at rebirth-linking is another, nevertheless, that [rebirth] is produced from that very [former state]; therefore, one is not released from evil kamma.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena!
This is the sixth dilemma: the identity and difference of name-and-form.
